    Sequential-section registration¶

    When two modalities come from neighbouring sections — spatial metabolomics (SM, MALDI) on one section, spatial transcriptomics (ST, Xenium) on the next — the tissue itself differs, so there is no one-to-one correspondence between cells. SMINT registers them as images instead: it rasterises both point clouds, and runs STalign's LDDMM (a smooth, invertible deformation) initialised from a handful of landmarks you place by hand. Every SM pixel then gets coordinates in the ST frame.

    In this tutorial you will:

    1. bring a mis-oriented synthetic SM section roughly into the ST frame with an orientation search (build_pretransform + overlap_score);
    2. rasterise both sections for landmarking (prepare_landmark_inputs) and look at the landmarks;
    3. register with register_sm_to_st (orientation="stalign") and measure the error against the known truth;
    4. register a downsampled real pair: Sample 2, Xenium section Z2 and MALDI section B, with its 11 landmarks.

    Runtime: each registration took about 20 s on one NVIDIA A30 GPU. On a CPU, LDDMM takes much longer — submit it as a job (see the end of this page). Requires: an environment with STalign, which needs numpy<2 and PyTorch.

    How this page was run: executed top to bottom on a GPU node with jupyter nbconvert --execute, from docs/tutorials/.

    Download this notebook: 03_sequential_registration.ipynb

    import logging
import sys
import time

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy.spatial import cKDTree

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s: %(message)s",
                    stream=sys.stdout, force=True)

from smint.alignment import (
    apply_pretransform, build_pretransform, describe_pretransform, load_landmarks,
    overlap_score, prepare_landmark_inputs, read_sm_matrix, register_sm_to_st,
    sm_coordinates,
)

ST, SM = "#2b6cb0", "#d53f8c"


def overlay(ax, st_xy, sm_xy, title, st_points=None, sm_points=None):
    """ST cells in blue, SM pixels in pink, optional numbered landmarks."""
    if len(st_xy):
        ax.scatter(st_xy[:, 0], st_xy[:, 1], s=0.4, c=ST, alpha=0.6, lw=0)
        ax.scatter([], [], s=20, c=ST, label="ST cells (Xenium)")
    if sm_xy is not None:
        ax.scatter(sm_xy[:, 0], sm_xy[:, 1], s=0.4, c=SM, alpha=0.25, lw=0)
        ax.scatter([], [], s=20, c=SM, label="SM pixels (MALDI)")
    for pts, colour in ((st_points, ST), (sm_points, SM)):
        if pts is not None:
            ax.scatter(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], s=60, marker="*", c="k")
            for i, (x, y) in enumerate(pts, 1):
                ax.annotate(str(i), (x, y), xytext=(4, 4), textcoords="offset points",
                            color=colour, fontsize=9, weight="bold")
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.invert_yaxis(); ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel("x (µm)"); ax.set_ylabel("y (µm)")
    ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9, markerscale=1)

    1. The synthetic pair¶

    synthetic_st.csv holds ST cell centroids in microns (x_final, y_final). synthetic_sm.csv holds SM pixels as raw pixel indices (x, y), like a MALDI export. read_sm_matrix converts pixels to microns with scale_xy (10 µm pixels here). Read without any rotation, the SM section lies on its side:

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    st = pd.read_csv("data/synthetic_st.csv")
st_xy = st[["x_final", "y_final"]].to_numpy()
sm_raw = read_sm_matrix("data/synthetic_sm.csv", scale_xy=10.0, verbose=False)
sm_raw_xy = sm_coordinates(sm_raw)
print(f"{len(st_xy):,} ST cells, {len(sm_raw_xy):,} SM pixels")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5))
overlay(axes[0], st_xy, None, "ST cells")
overlay(axes[1], np.empty((0, 2)), sm_raw_xy, "SM pixels, read with scale_xy=10 (no rotation)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
    st = pd.read_csv("data/synthetic_st.csv") st_xy = st[["x_final", "y_final"]].to_numpy() sm_raw = read_sm_matrix("data/synthetic_sm.csv", scale_xy=10.0, verbose=False) sm_raw_xy = sm_coordinates(sm_raw) print(f"{len(st_xy):,} ST cells, {len(sm_raw_xy):,} SM pixels") fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5)) overlay(axes[0], st_xy, None, "ST cells") overlay(axes[1], np.empty((0, 2)), sm_raw_xy, "SM pixels, read with scale_xy=10 (no rotation)") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

    2. Coarse pre-registration: find the orientation¶

    build_pretransform builds a flip / rotation / scale about the source centroid and moves it onto the target's centroid; overlap_score is the fraction of 50 µm bins occupied by the target that the moved source also occupies. Trying every 15° with and without flips and keeping the best score is what smint-alignment pretransform --search does:

    In [3]:
    Copied! 
    best = (-1.0, None)
for flip_x in (False, True):
    for flip_y in (False, True):
        for rotation in range(-180, 180, 15):
            matrix = build_pretransform(sm_raw_xy, st_xy, rotation=float(rotation),
                                        flip_x=flip_x, flip_y=flip_y)
            score = overlap_score(apply_pretransform(sm_raw_xy, matrix), st_xy)
            if score > best[0]:
                best = (score, dict(rotation=rotation, flip_x=flip_x, flip_y=flip_y))
score, settings = best
print(f"best: {settings}, overlap {score:.3f}")
matrix = build_pretransform(sm_raw_xy, st_xy, **settings)
{k: (round(v, 3) if isinstance(v, float) else v) for k, v in describe_pretransform(matrix).items()}
    best = (-1.0, None) for flip_x in (False, True): for flip_y in (False, True): for rotation in range(-180, 180, 15): matrix = build_pretransform(sm_raw_xy, st_xy, rotation=float(rotation), flip_x=flip_x, flip_y=flip_y) score = overlap_score(apply_pretransform(sm_raw_xy, matrix), st_xy) if score > best[0]: best = (score, dict(rotation=rotation, flip_x=flip_x, flip_y=flip_y)) score, settings = best print(f"best: {settings}, overlap {score:.3f}") matrix = build_pretransform(sm_raw_xy, st_xy, **settings) {k: (round(v, 3) if isinstance(v, float) else v) for k, v in describe_pretransform(matrix).items()}
    best: {'rotation': 90, 'flip_x': False, 'flip_y': False}, overlap 0.921
    Out[3]:
    {'scale_x': 1.068,
 'scale_y': 1.068,
 'rotation_deg': 90.0,
 'shear_deg': 0.0,
 'translation': (3839.6063820897325, -93.48855425776478),
 'determinant': 1.141,
 'reflects': False}

    The search finds a 90° counter-clockwise rotation. That is the rotation MALDI exports need relative to Xenium on this setup, and read_sm_matrix applies it directly with rotate_left_90=True. The remaining few degrees, the scale difference and the warp are left to the landmarks and LDDMM. The landmark files below were placed in the frame that read_sm_matrix(scale_xy=10, rotate_left_90=True) produces, so that is what every later step passes.

    In [4]:

moved = apply_pretransform(sm_raw_xy, matrix)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5))
overlay(axes[0], st_xy, moved, f"Best search result (overlap {score:.2f})")
overlay(axes[1], st_xy, sm_xy, "rotate_left_90=True, no other change")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

    3. Landmarks¶

    LDDMM needs a starting point: a few landmarks, the same recognisable features picked in both sections in the same order (correspondence is by position in the list). prepare_landmark_inputs rasterises both sections at dx µm per pixel and writes the .npz images that STalign's point_annotator.py opens; the SMINT napari plugin (3. Landmarks) does the same interactively.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    inputs = prepare_landmark_inputs(
    st_file="data/synthetic_st.csv",
    sm_file="data/synthetic_sm.csv",
    output_prefix="landmarks/synthetic",      # writes landmarks/synthetic_st.npz, _sm.npz
    dx=30.0,
    sm_kwargs=sm_kwargs,
)
{k: inputs[k] for k in ("st_npz", "sm_npz", "st_points", "sm_points")}
    inputs = prepare_landmark_inputs( st_file="data/synthetic_st.csv", sm_file="data/synthetic_sm.csv", output_prefix="landmarks/synthetic", # writes landmarks/synthetic_st.npz, _sm.npz dx=30.0, sm_kwargs=sm_kwargs, ) {k: inputs[k] for k in ("st_npz", "sm_npz", "st_points", "sm_points")}

    point_annotator.py saves each picked set as <stem>_points.npy, a {label: [(x, y)]} dictionary. The tutorial data ships with 8 landmark pairs in that format. load_landmarks reads them in STalign's row-column (y, x) order, so swap the columns back to plot them:

    4. Register¶

    register_sm_to_st rasterises both sections again, runs LDDMM with the SM as source and the ST as target, starting from the landmark fit, and transforms every SM pixel. Pass orientation="stalign" to get true (x, y) in the ST frame, which is what you want to overlay or join with the ST data. (lddmm_params={"draw": False} turns off STalign's own progress figures.)

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    start = time.time()
registered = register_sm_to_st(
    st_file="data/synthetic_st.csv",
    sm_file="data/synthetic_sm.csv",
    st_points_file="data/synthetic_st_points.npy",
    sm_points_file="data/synthetic_sm_points.npy",
    sm_kwargs=sm_kwargs,
    orientation="stalign",
    output_path="registered/synthetic_sm_transformed.csv",
    lddmm_params={"draw": False},
)
print(f"registered {len(registered):,} SM pixels in {time.time() - start:.0f} s")
registered.head(3)
    start = time.time() registered = register_sm_to_st( st_file="data/synthetic_st.csv", sm_file="data/synthetic_sm.csv", st_points_file="data/synthetic_st_points.npy", sm_points_file="data/synthetic_sm_points.npy", sm_kwargs=sm_kwargs, orientation="stalign", output_path="registered/synthetic_sm_transformed.csv", lddmm_params={"draw": False}, ) print(f"registered {len(registered):,} SM pixels in {time.time() - start:.0f} s") registered.head(3)

    The output is the SM table with two columns added, x_transformed and y_transformed; every other column (for real data, one per m/z) is kept.

    The synthetic data comes with the true ST-frame position of every SM pixel, so the error can be measured — and compared with what the landmarks alone give (a least-squares affine through the 8 pairs):

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    truth = pd.read_csv("data/synthetic_sm_truth.csv")[["x_true", "y_true"]].to_numpy()
after = registered[["x_transformed", "y_transformed"]].to_numpy()

design = np.column_stack([sm_lm, np.ones(len(sm_lm))])
affine = np.linalg.lstsq(design, st_lm, rcond=None)[0]
landmarks_only = np.column_stack([sm_xy, np.ones(len(sm_xy))]) @ affine

for name, xy in (("landmark affine only", landmarks_only), ("LDDMM", after)):
    err = np.linalg.norm(xy - truth, axis=1)
    print(f"{name:>21}: median error {np.median(err):5.1f} um, 90th percentile {np.percentile(err, 90):5.1f} um")
    truth = pd.read_csv("data/synthetic_sm_truth.csv")[["x_true", "y_true"]].to_numpy() after = registered[["x_transformed", "y_transformed"]].to_numpy() design = np.column_stack([sm_lm, np.ones(len(sm_lm))]) affine = np.linalg.lstsq(design, st_lm, rcond=None)[0] landmarks_only = np.column_stack([sm_xy, np.ones(len(sm_xy))]) @ affine for name, xy in (("landmark affine only", landmarks_only), ("LDDMM", after)): err = np.linalg.norm(xy - truth, axis=1) print(f"{name:>21}: median error {np.median(err):5.1f} um, 90th percentile {np.percentile(err, 90):5.1f} um")
     landmark affine only: median error  34.9 um, 90th percentile  56.1 um
                LDDMM: median error  28.5 um, 90th percentile  69.4 um

    Copied! 
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5))
overlay(axes[0], st_xy, sm_xy, "Before registration (rotate_left_90 only)")
overlay(axes[1], st_xy, after, "After STalign LDDMM")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5)) overlay(axes[0], st_xy, sm_xy, "Before registration (rotate_left_90 only)") overlay(axes[1], st_xy, after, "After STalign LDDMM") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

    LDDMM brings the median error below the landmark fit, to about one 30 µm raster pixel — but not everywhere: compare the 90th percentiles. Coordinates alone carry little information inside the tissue (the SM raster above is flat), so LDDMM mostly matches the outline and the holes; the landmarks carry the rest. Spread them over the whole section, on features you can find in both modalities, and always check the overlay.

    5. Real data: Sample 2, Xenium Z2 and MALDI section B¶

    The real pair: 53,622 Xenium cells from section Z2, and a random quarter of the MALDI pixels from neighbouring section B (coordinates only), with the 11 landmark pairs placed for this registration. The MALDI pixels need the same scale_xy=10 and rotate_left_90=True.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    st_real = pd.read_csv("data/sample2_st_z2.csv")[["x_final", "y_final"]].to_numpy()
sm_real = sm_coordinates(read_sm_matrix("data/sample2_sm_sectionB.csv", verbose=False, **sm_kwargs))
st_lm = load_landmarks("data/sample2_st_landmarks.npy")[:, ::-1]
sm_lm = load_landmarks("data/sample2_sm_landmarks.npy")[:, ::-1]
print(f"{len(st_real):,} ST cells, {len(sm_real):,} SM pixels, {len(st_lm)} landmark pairs")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 6))
overlay(axes[0], st_real, None, "ST (Xenium Z2)", st_points=st_lm)
overlay(axes[1], np.empty((0, 2)), sm_real, "SM (MALDI section B)", sm_points=sm_lm)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
    st_real = pd.read_csv("data/sample2_st_z2.csv")[["x_final", "y_final"]].to_numpy() sm_real = sm_coordinates(read_sm_matrix("data/sample2_sm_sectionB.csv", verbose=False, **sm_kwargs)) st_lm = load_landmarks("data/sample2_st_landmarks.npy")[:, ::-1] sm_lm = load_landmarks("data/sample2_sm_landmarks.npy")[:, ::-1] print(f"{len(st_real):,} ST cells, {len(sm_real):,} SM pixels, {len(st_lm)} landmark pairs") fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 6)) overlay(axes[0], st_real, None, "ST (Xenium Z2)", st_points=st_lm) overlay(axes[1], np.empty((0, 2)), sm_real, "SM (MALDI section B)", sm_points=sm_lm) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

    INFO: LDDMM alignment complete

    INFO: Saved transformed data to registered/sample2_sm_transformed.csv

    registered 115,502 SM pixels in 17 s

    There is no ground truth between two different sections. The practical checks are the overlay, and how far each SM pixel lands from the nearest ST cell:

    In [12]:
    Copied! 
    after = registered[["x_transformed", "y_transformed"]].to_numpy()
distance, _ = cKDTree(st_real).query(after)
print(f"median distance to the nearest ST cell: {np.median(distance):.1f} um")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 6))
overlay(axes[0], st_real, sm_real, "Before registration")
overlay(axes[1], st_real, after, "After STalign LDDMM")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
    after = registered[["x_transformed", "y_transformed"]].to_numpy() distance, _ = cKDTree(st_real).query(after) print(f"median distance to the nearest ST cell: {np.median(distance):.1f} um") fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 6)) overlay(axes[0], st_real, sm_real, "Before registration") overlay(axes[1], st_real, after, "After STalign LDDMM") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
    median distance to the nearest ST cell: 16.4 um

    That is about half a 30 µm raster pixel, the same as the full-resolution registration of this pair in the worked examples.

    Orientation: why stalign¶

    STalign works in row-column order. orientation="dataset" — the default, kept so older outputs can be reproduced — returns the two transformed axes the other way round, transposed relative to the ST cells. Swapping the columns of the result above shows what that looks like over the ST data: like a failed registration, although the registration is fine.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 6))
overlay(ax, st_real, after[:, ::-1], 'What orientation="dataset" gives')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 6)) overlay(ax, st_real, after[:, ::-1], 'What orientation="dataset" gives') plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

    Run it as a job¶

    LDDMM belongs on a GPU node. From a login node, the command line builds the job, submits it with sbatch and, with --watch, waits for the result. Point --worker-python at the environment that has STalign:

    smint-alignment st-sm \
    --st data/sample2_st_z2.csv \
    --sm data/sample2_sm_sectionB.csv \
    --st-points data/sample2_st_landmarks.npy \
    --sm-points data/sample2_sm_landmarks.npy \
    --rotate-left-90 --orientation stalign \
    --output-dir sample2_z2_registration \
    --submit --watch --partition gpuq --gpus 1 --memory 64G \
    --worker-python /path/to/stalign-env/bin/python

    The output directory must be on storage the compute node can see. The napari plugin's 4. Register widget submits the same job. See Running on HPC.
